blocks.content: The story starts at 3:47 AM on a Tuesday.

Your API is humming along at its normal 2,000 requests per minute. Then a single client one badly written mobile app that just pushed an update to 2 million users starts retrying a failed request in a tight loop. Within 30 seconds, your API is receiving 800,000 requests per minute. Your database connection pool exhausts. Your servers run out of memory. Your entire platform goes down for every user, not just the broken app.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520242-22228355.png
blocks.alt: A single retrying client overwhelming the API and exhausting database connections

blocks.content: This is why rate limiting exists. Not just to be fair but to be alive.

Rate limiting is a control mechanism that restricts how many requests a client can make in a given time window. It protects your infrastructure, enforces fair usage, prevents abuse, and gives you a lever to monetise your API through tiers. Without it, any single bad actor whether malicious or simply buggy can take down your entire system.
1. What rate limiting actually protects against
blocks.text: 1. What rate limiting actually protects against

blocks.content: Rate limiting defends against four distinct threat categories, each with different characteristics.

["Abuse and attacks: a malicious actor hammering your login endpoint to brute-force passwords, scraping your entire product catalogue, or running a credential stuffing attack using a list of leaked credentials from another breach.
","Buggy clients: the honest mistake. A mobile app that retries on network failure without exponential backoff. A webhook receiver that accidentally loops. A cron job that fires every second instead of every minute. These cause the same damage as attacks.
","Resource hogging: one customer on your shared API tier consuming 90% of capacity, causing degraded service for everyone else. Not malicious, just inconsiderate.
","Cascading failures: when one downstream service slows down, upstream callers retry more aggressively, generating even more load, making the slowdown worse. Rate limiting breaks this feedback loop.
"]
items: Abuse and attacks: a malicious actor hammering your login endpoint to brute-force passwords, scraping your entire product catalogue, or running a credential stuffing attack using a list of leaked credentials from another breach.

Buggy clients: the honest mistake. A mobile app that retries on network failure without exponential backoff. A webhook receiver that accidentally loops. A cron job that fires every second instead of every minute. These cause the same damage as attacks.
Resource hogging: one customer on your shared API tier consuming 90% of capacity, causing degraded service for everyone else. Not malicious, just inconsiderate.
Cascading failures: when one downstream service slows down, upstream callers retry more aggressively, generating even more load, making the slowdown worse. Rate limiting breaks this feedback loop.

blocks.content: 2. Where rate limiting lives in your architecture
blocks.text: 2. Where rate limiting lives in your architecture

blocks.content: Before the algorithms, understand that rate limiting can happen at multiple layers simultaneously and each layer catches different things.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520242-696659322.png
blocks.alt: Rate limiting enforced at CDN gateway and application layers as defence in depth

blocks.content: Defence in depth. The CDN catches the flood before it hits your infrastructure. The API Gateway enforces quotas per client. The application layer enforces business rules. Each layer is a checkpoint that the next layer never has to deal with.
3. The 5 RL algorithms
Each algorithm controls request rates differently, balancing accuracy, performance, and resource usage.
Algorithm 1: Fixed Window Counter
The Fixed Window Counter is the simplest rate-limiting algorithm.
It divides time into fixed windows, such as 1 minute. For each user, the system counts how many requests are made during the current window. If the count exceeds the limit, the request is rejected.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520242-504069831.png
blocks.alt: Fixed window counter checking request count against the limit for the current window

blocks.content: For example, suppose the limit is 100 requests per minute.

["Between 12:00 and 12:01, a user sends 50 requests.
","Between 12:01 and 12:02, the same user sends another 50 requests.
"]
items: Between 12:00 and 12:01, a user sends 50 requests.
Between 12:01 and 12:02, the same user sends another 50 requests.

blocks.content: Both windows are within their limits, so all requests are allowed.

The problem occurs at the window boundary. A user can send 50 requests at 12:00:55 and another 50 requests at 12:01:05. Although only 10 seconds have passed, the user has effectively sent 100 requests in 10 seconds.
This is called the Boundary Burst Problem because requests are concentrated around the boundary between two windows.

The implementation is very simple. Redis stores a counter for the current time window. Every request increments the counter. If the counter exceeds the limit, the server returns HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests). When the window expires, Redis automatically removes the counter and a new window starts.
Implementation in Redis:

key = "rate:{user_id}:{endpoint}:{current_minute}"

count = INCR key

if count == 1: EXPIRE key 60
if count > limit: return 429

blocks.content: Algorithm 2: Sliding Window Log
The Sliding Window Log solves the boundary burst problem of the Fixed Window Counter.

Instead of storing a single counter, it stores a timestamp for every request. When a new request arrives, the system looks at the last N seconds and counts how many requests were made during that period.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520243-703384820.png
blocks.alt: Sliding window log storing timestamps and counting requests in the last N seconds

blocks.content: For example, suppose the limit is 100 requests per minute.

A user sends 100 requests between 12:00:10 and 12:01:10. When the 101st request arrives, the system checks the last 60 seconds. If 100 requests already exist in that window, the new request is rejected.
The window is always moving with time, which is why it is called a sliding window.
Accurate: no boundary burst problem. The window truly slides with every request. The cost: memory.

You store one timestamp per request, per user. If a user makes 10,000 requests per hour, you store 10,000 timestamps. At scale with millions of users, this becomes expensive. Mostly used when you need precision and can afford the memory.
Algorithm 3: Sliding Window Counter
The Sliding Window Counter is a practical middle ground between the Fixed Window Counter and the Sliding Window Log.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276843991-255450803.png
blocks.alt: Sliding window counter combining current and previous window counts into a weighted estimate

blocks.content: Instead of storing every request timestamp, it keeps only two counters:
["Current Window Count","Previous Window Count"]
items: Current Window Count
Previous Window Count

blocks.content: When a new request arrives, the system calculates an estimated request count by combining the current window count and a weighted portion of the previous window count.
For example, suppose the rate limit window is 60 seconds. You are 15 seconds into the current window. The previous window had 80 requests, and the current window has 20 requests.
Since only 15 seconds have passed, some traffic from the previous window still affects the current rate. The system combines both counts and estimates the actual request rate as 80 requests.
This approach closely approximates a true sliding window without storing individual request timestamps.
Keeps counts in two windows (current and previous) and interpolates based on how far into the current window you are.
rate = prev_count × (1 - elapsed/window) + curr_count
If the window is 60 seconds, you're 15 seconds in, prev had 80 requests, curr has 20:

This approximates the true sliding window count with just two integer counters. Memory efficient, accurate enough for most use cases (within ~0.003% of true sliding window). This is what Cloudflare and most production rate limiters use.
Algorithm 4: Token Bucket

The most widely used algorithm in production. Imagine a bucket that holds tokens. The bucket fills at a constant rate (say 10 tokens per second). Each request consumes one token. If there are tokens, the request is allowed. If the bucket is empty, the request is rejected.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520243-550490466.png
blocks.alt: Token bucket filling at a constant rate and requests consuming tokens

blocks.content: Token bucket's key advantage: it naturally handles bursts. A client that makes occasional bursts (a mobile app that syncs when the user wakes up) is treated more fairly than a client that hammers continuously.
The bucket accumulates tokens during idle periods and can spend them on a burst. But sustained throughput above the refill rate is impossible the bucket empties and stays empty.

This is why AWS, Stripe, GitHub, and most major APIs use token bucket. It matches real-world usage patterns: clients often have bursty behaviour, and punishing legitimate bursts creates a poor developer experience.
Algorithm 5: Leaky Bucket
The inverse of token bucket. Requests arrive at any rate and enter a queue (the bucket). The queue drains at a constant rate to the backend. Requests that overflow the queue are rejected.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276847360-572650527.png
blocks.alt: Leaky bucket queue draining requests to the backend at a constant rate

blocks.content: Leaky bucket guarantees a perfectly smooth output rate your backend never sees a spike.

The trade-off: legitimate bursts get queued and delayed. If a user sends 10 requests at once and the drain rate is 2/sec, request 1 goes immediately, request 2 waits 500ms, request 3 waits 1 second, and so on.
Users experience artificial latency even when the system is lightly loaded.
Used for: network traffic shaping, protecting downstream services with hard throughput limits, smoothing video streaming bitrate. Not great for interactive APIs where latency matters.
4. Algorithm comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520244-938942764.png
blocks.alt: Choosing between fixed window sliding log sliding counter token bucket and leaky bucket algorithms

blocks.content: 5. Choosing the Rate Limiting Key
The algorithm is only half the design. The other half is deciding what identifies a client for rate limiting purposes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276850708-723688206.png
blocks.alt: Choosing a rate limiting key from IP address user ID or API key

blocks.content: When implementing rate limiting, the first question is: what should we count requests against?
1. IP Address
Here, requests are limited based on the client's IP address.

This works well for public APIs and DDoS protection because no authentication is required. However, it is easy to bypass using VPNs or rotating IPs. It can also unfairly rate limit multiple users sharing the same office or home network.
2. API Key / Token
Here, requests are limited per API key.

This is commonly used in developer APIs like Stripe, GitHub, and Twilio. Each API key gets its own quota regardless of the user's IP address. It is easy to manage and can support different limits for different pricing plans.
3. User ID
Here, requests are limited per logged-in user.
The limit is tied to the account, not the device or IP address. Even if the user changes devices or networks, the same rate limit applies. This works well for consumer applications.
4. User + Endpoint (Most Common)
Here, requests are limited using both the user and the API endpoint.
This allows different limits for different operations. For example:
["Search API → 10 requests/minute","Read API → 100 requests/minute","Write API → 50 requests/minute"]
items: Search API → 10 requests/minute
Read API → 100 requests/minute
Write API → 50 requests/minute

blocks.content: This is the most flexible and commonly used approach in production systems.
6. Distributed rate limiting ( The hard problem )
blocks.text: 6. Distributed rate limiting ( The hard problem )

blocks.content: A single server can rate limit trivially keep a counter in memory. The moment you have multiple gateway instances (which you always do in production), the problem becomes hard. Each instance only sees its own traffic. If a user makes 6 requests and three go to server A and three go to server B, each server sees only 3 and thinks the limit of 5 hasn't been hit.
Problem: Local Counters
The user sends requests through multiple gateway servers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276852308-911923270.png
blocks.alt: Per server local counters failing to enforce a shared limit across gateway servers

blocks.content: Suppose the rate limit is 5 requests, but the user sends 10 requests.
Some requests reach GW-1, some reach GW-2, and others reach GW-3. Each gateway maintains its own local counter and only sees the traffic that arrives at that server.
As a result:
["GW-1 sees only 3 requests.","GW-2 sees only 4 requests.","GW-3 sees only 3 requests."]
items: GW-1 sees only 3 requests.
GW-2 sees only 4 requests.
GW-3 sees only 3 requests.

blocks.content: Since none of the servers individually see more than 5 requests, all requests are allowed.
However, globally the user actually made 10 requests, which should have exceeded the limit. The rate limiter fails because the counters are distributed across servers.
Solution: Centralized Redis
The gateway servers no longer maintain their own counters. Instead, every request is sent to a shared Redis instance.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520722-583812822.png
blocks.alt: Gateway servers sharing a single Redis counter to enforce a global rate limit

blocks.content: When a request arrives:

["The gateway receives the request.","The gateway increments the user's counter in Redis.","Redis returns the updated count.","If the count is below the limit, the request is allowed.","If the count exceeds the limit, the request is rejected."]
items: The gateway receives the request.
The gateway increments the user's counter in Redis.
Redis returns the updated count.
If the count is below the limit, the request is allowed.
If the count exceeds the limit, the request is rejected.

blocks.content: Because all gateways use the same Redis counter, Redis always knows the true global request count.
For example:
["Request 1 → Redis count = 1","Request 2 → Redis count = 2","...","Request 10 → Redis count = 10"]
items: Request 1 → Redis count = 1
Request 2 → Redis count = 2
Request 10 → Redis count = 10

blocks.content: Now the rate limit is enforced correctly regardless of which gateway receives the request.
Why Redis? Trade-off and Approximate Local Sync
blocks.text: Why Redis? Trade-off and Approximate Local Sync

blocks.content: Redis is commonly used for distributed rate limiting because it provides a shared, atomic, and globally accurate counter that can be accessed by all gateway servers.
The trade-off is that every request requires a network call to Redis, adding a small latency and increasing Redis load.
At very high scale, systems often use Approximate Local Sync, where each gateway maintains a local counter and periodically synchronizes with Redis.
This reduces Redis traffic and improves performance but may allow a small number of extra requests during synchronization windows, making it slightly less accurate.

["X-RateLimit-Limit :  what the limit is. Client knows what they're working with.
","X-RateLimit-Remaining :  how many requests they have left in the current window.
","X-RateLimit-Reset : Unix timestamp when the window resets. Client can schedule retry.
","Retry-After :  seconds until they can try again. Standard HTTP header. Well-behaved clients use this to back off automatically.

items: X-RateLimit-Limit :  what the limit is. Client knows what they're working with.
X-RateLimit-Remaining :  how many requests they have left in the current window.
X-RateLimit-Reset : Unix timestamp when the window resets. Client can schedule retry.
Retry-After :  seconds until they can try again. Standard HTTP header. Well-behaved clients use this to back off automatically.

blocks.content: Include these headers on every successful response too not just 429s. This lets clients self-police. If remaining drops to 10, a smart client can slow down proactively instead of hitting the limit.
8. Rate limiting tiers
Rate limiting is not just protection it's a business model. API tiers are almost always expressed as rate limits.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785276855744-95696125.png
blocks.alt: Rate limit tiers based on the API key tier free pro or enterprise

blocks.content: The rate limit key includes the API key's tier.

When the API key is validated, the gateway fetches the tier and applies the corresponding limit. An enterprise customer on a dedicated infrastructure bypass hits no shared rate limit at all their limit is enforced at a different layer entirely.
9. Production Edge Cases in Rate Limiting
blocks.text: 9. Production Edge Cases in Rate Limiting

blocks.content:
["Redis Failure: If Redis goes down, the rate limiter stops working. Most systems choose fail open, meaning requests are temporarily allowed instead of bringing down the entire API. A circuit breaker and alerts are usually added so the team is notified immediately.
","VPN and NAT Users: IP-based rate limiting is easy to bypass using VPNs or rotating IPs. For authenticated APIs, it's better to rate limit using User ID or API Key instead of IP addresses.
","First-Party App Bursts: Your own mobile app may send many requests when it starts. If rate limits are too strict, users may see errors. A common solution is to batch requests or give internal applications higher limits.
","Retry Storms: When users receive a 429 Too Many Requests response, they may all retry at the same time, creating another traffic spike. To avoid this, systems add jitter, so clients retry at slightly different times.
","Expensive APIs: Not all APIs cost the same. A simple read request is cheap, while operations like generating reports or exporting data are expensive. These endpoints should have much stricter rate limits than normal APIs."]
items: Redis Failure: If Redis goes down, the rate limiter stops working. Most systems choose fail open, meaning requests are temporarily allowed instead of bringing down the entire API. A circuit breaker and alerts are usually added so the team is notified immediately.
VPN and NAT Users: IP-based rate limiting is easy to bypass using VPNs or rotating IPs. For authenticated APIs, it's better to rate limit using User ID or API Key instead of IP addresses.

First-Party App Bursts: Your own mobile app may send many requests when it starts. If rate limits are too strict, users may see errors. A common solution is to batch requests or give internal applications higher limits.

Retry Storms: When users receive a 429 Too Many Requests response, they may all retry at the same time, creating another traffic spike. To avoid this, systems add jitter, so clients retry at slightly different times.

Expensive APIs: Not all APIs cost the same. A simple read request is cheap, while operations like generating reports or exporting data are expensive. These endpoints should have much stricter rate limits than normal APIs.

blocks.content: 10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About Rate Limiting
blocks.text: 10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About Rate Limiting

blocks.content: When asked how to protect an API from abuse, start by saying you would use a Token Bucket algorithm because it allows short bursts of traffic while still enforcing an average request rate.

Next, explain that rate limits should be applied using a key such as API Key, User ID, or User + Endpoint. Different endpoints can have different limits. For example, a search API may allow 10 requests per minute, while a normal read API may allow 1000 requests per minute.

Since the system runs on multiple servers, local counters won't work because each server only sees part of the traffic. Instead, use a centralized Redis cluster where all servers update the same counter.
When a user exceeds the limit, return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) along with Retry-After and rate-limit headers so clients know when they can retry.

If Redis becomes unavailable, most systems fail open, meaning requests are temporarily allowed while alerts are sent to the engineering team. This avoids taking down the entire API because of a rate limiter failure.
For paid APIs, limits can be tied to subscription plans. Free users get lower limits, while premium or enterprise customers get higher limits.
Interview Takeaway
A strong answer usually sounds like:

"I would use a Token Bucket rate limiter backed by Redis. The limit would be applied per API key or user, with different limits for different endpoints. Exceeded requests would return HTTP 429. Since the system is distributed, Redis provides a shared counter across all gateway instances. If Redis fails, I would fail open and alert the team. Different pricing tiers would have different rate limits."
